content: Glechoma hederacea, commonly known as Ground-ivy, is a perennial, aromatic, evergreen creeping plant belonging to the mint family, Lamiaceae. It is native to Europe and southwestern Asia but has been introduced to North America, where it is now widespread except in the Rocky Mountains. This plant is known by various names, including Alehoof, Creeping Charlie, Catsfoot (due to the shape and size of its leaves), Field Balm, Run-away-robin, Gill-over-the-ground, and Tunhoof. It is sometimes referred to as Creeping Jenny, though this name more commonly applies to Lysimachia nummularia. The plant is characterized by its round to kidney-shaped (reniform) leaves with crenate (rounded toothed) edges. These leaves are 2-3 cm in diameter and are attached to square stems via petioles that are 3-6 cm long. The stems root at their nodes, allowing the plant to spread. Glechoma hederacea is a variable species, with its size ranging from 5 cm to 50 cm depending on environmental conditions. It is often mistaken for common mallow (Malva neglecta) due to the similarity in leaf shape. However, mallow leaves are attached to the stem at the back of the leaf, whereas Ground-ivy leaves are attached at the center. Additionally, Ground-ivy has square stems, a hairy upper leaf surface, and a distinctive minty odor when damaged. Unlike mallow, Ground-ivy spreads via nodes on its stems. The flowers of Glechoma hederacea are bilaterally symmetrical, funnel-shaped, and range in color from blue to bluish-violet or lavender. They grow in clusters of two or three in the leaf axils near the upper part of the stem or its tip. The plant typically blooms in the spring. It thrives in moist, shaded areas but can also tolerate full sun. It is commonly found in grasslands, wooded areas, wastelands, lawns, and around buildings, as it can survive mowing. The plant spreads through stolons and seeds, forming dense mats that can dominate lawns, making it an invasive or aggressive weed. Ecological Aspects Glechoma hederacea serves as a nectar source for various wild bees, including species such as Anthophora furcata, Anthidum manicatum, Anthophora plumipes, Anthophora quadrimaculata, Osmia aurulenta, Osmia caerulentes, and Osmia uncinata. Cultivation and Uses Although often considered a weed due to its invasive nature, Glechoma hederacea is sometimes cultivated as a potted plant or ground cover. A variegated variety is occasionally available commercially. Historically, the plant was brought to North America by European settlers for its culinary and medicinal properties. The fresh herb can be steeped in hot water to make an herbal tea rich in vitamin C. The plant’s essential oil has potent medicinal properties and has been used for centuries as a general remedy for colds, coughs, and mucous membrane congestion. It also exhibits anti-inflammatory effects and has been claimed to promote the excretion of lead in urine. The medicinal use of Glechoma hederacea dates back millennia. Galen, the ancient Greek physician, recommended it for treating eye inflammation. John Gerard, an English herbalist, suggested its use for tinnitus, as well as for its diuretic, astringent, tonic, and gentle stimulant properties. It was also used for kidney diseases, indigestion, and as a lung herb. Additionally, the Saxons used the plant in brewing beer for flavoring, clarification, and preservation before hops became the standard ingredient. This historical use is reflected in names like Alehoof, Tunhoof, and Gill-over-the-ground. Control Glechoma hederacea is widely recognized as a weed, particularly in fertile, moist soils with low boron content. It thrives in shady areas where grass struggles to grow but can also be problematic in full sun. Small infestations can be managed through hand weeding, though repeated efforts are necessary due to the plant’s rhizomatous growth, which allows it to regenerate from roots or stem fragments. The plant is highly sensitive to boron, and a solution of borax (sodium tetraborate) can be used to control it. A recommended mixture is 8-10 ounces of borax dissolved in 4 ounces of warm water, diluted to 2.5 gallons of solution, and applied evenly over 1,000 square feet of lawn. However, boron is toxic to other plants and animals at slightly higher concentrations and does not degrade in the environment, potentially causing long-term soil and groundwater issues. Commercial herbicides are another option for controlling Glechoma hederacea. There is some debate about the effectiveness of different herbicides, with dicamba (found in products like Trimec and Weed-B-Gon) and 2,4-D being described as both effective and ineffective by various sources. This variability may be due to differences in application rates or the existence of subpopulations with varying susceptibilities. To prevent herbicide resistance, it is recommended to rotate products rather than using the same one repeatedly. Triclopyr has been reported as effective, while Clopyralid, MCPP, and quinclorac are generally considered ineffective. Fluroxypyr and Confront have also been described as effective, though their sale is restricted to professionals. Two applications of herbicide, spaced 10-14 days apart, are typically required. Surviving plants may regenerate after 24 days, necessitating a second treatment 4-5 weeks later and potentially additional follow-ups. The timing of application is also critical; fall is generally the best time for broadleaf herbicides, though slow-acting herbicides like triclopyr may not show results until the following growing season. Other control methods include applying more than 2 pounds of nitrogen per 1,000 square feet annually and using the pre-emergence herbicide isoxaben. In severe cases, a full-spectrum herbicide like glyphosate (e.g., Roundup) may be used to kill the entire lawn, which can then be reseeded.
